detail.abstract: An agent that chooses for a person is asked to do four things at once: follow the mandate it was given, keep up as the person changes, ignore parties who hold no mandate, and act without asking. This paper develops the second component of the Theory of Delegated Markets, the Delegation Possibility Frontier, as a testable claim about the governance of AI agents. I define the four objectives (fidelity, adaptation, resistance to manipulation, and autonomy) as measurable properties of an architecture, meaning an agent with whatever human review it carries, each read on executed choices against a benchmark outside the agent. Four boundary conditions are premises, not results: mandate incompleteness, unannounced change, manipulable outside evidence, and preference endogeneity. Within them I conjecture that the best attainable values of the four objectives cannot be reached together, so every architecture sits on a frontier. Six pairwise tensions, LAD1 to LAD6, give the conjecture its content, each with a mechanism, a boundary, and a falsifier; the adaptation and autonomy pair is a lemma drawn from change detection. Public procurement and deployed shopping agents show opposite designs, each in its 2 own environment: procurement resists by fixing its rule for the life of a tender, while shopping agents read outside text, are moved by it, and may lie inside their frontier. Better technologies of verification and of the principal's input move the frontier; review thresholds, reversibility, bounded mandates, and update rules choose a point on it; audit trails measure where an architecture sits. I state the formal program a proof would need and leave the proof open. One architecture that provably attains all four maxima under the four conditions would refute the conjecture.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for conceptualising financial literacy beyond the conventional mathematical and formalist approaches that dominate the literature. The Financial Literacy Framework presented herein comprises the Financial Literacy Stick (FLS)-composed ko of awareness, action, and results components-and three distinct Platforms: the Finance Platform, the Goods (and/or Services) Platform, and the Combined Platform. Each Platform operates across three levels corresponding to the acquisition of availability, the acquisition of financing or goods, and the efficient use thereof. The framework posits that financial literacy operates through continuous interactions between awareness and action, generating results that move vertically, horizontally, or diagonally across Platforms within a strategic time horizon. Furthermore, the paper situates finance as a subset of economics, delineating personal finance, general finance, and economics as corresponding to the three levels of the framework. The paper extends the framework to monetary policy, arguing that in developed economies, mature monetary policy frameworks mean the FLS acts mainly at the bottom levels and platform movement is faster, while in developing economies awareness and institutional frictions impede transmission. Authoritative information, in both best-developed and worst-developing economies, is sensitive and must be communicated in a predetermined structure to be clear. The Bernanke "taper tantrum" of 2013 is examined as a case of miscommunication that illustrates the costs of failing to observe such structure. This tripartite structure offers a comprehensive lens for analysing how economic agents with varying levels of financial literacy interact with financing methods, goods, and services to achieve efficiency in resource allocation.

detail.abstract: Discussion of the book "Immigration Realities: Challenging Common Misconceptions," in which Ernesto Castañeda and Carina Cione use an evidence-based and practical interdisciplinary approach to break down the most prevalent false claims about immigration. The book works as a comprehensive guide for the reader to understand the basics and complexities of immigration in an accessible way, written in such a way that even those who consider themselves knowledgeable on the topic will come away with important takeaways. Presenting decades of research, as well as original insights from research conducted in El Paso, Texas, Immigration Realities provides the context needed to understand how immigration affects economies, crime rates, and social welfare systems across diverse places, ethnic groups, and historical eras. Each chapter focuses on one particular immigration myth, providing empirical data to dispel it.

title: Reasoning Depth As A Decision Variable in Generative AI

detail.title: Reasoning Depth As A Decision Variable in Generative AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: An unexpected methodological issue emerged during the 2026 NFL Pick'em study: the reasoning level selected in ChatGPT may materially alter the structure of an AI-generated decision even when the basic recommendation remains largely unchanged. A Week 7 side experiment compared three independent ChatGPT runs using High, Medium, and Instant reasoning. Each run was conducted in a fresh chat, within seconds of the others, using essentially the same simple instruction: make the Week 7 NFL Pick'em selections and rank the teams by confidence. The result was striking. The three configurations agreed on the winner in 13 of 14 games, suggesting substantial stability in first-order selection. Yet their confidence rankings differed dramatically. Kansas City was ranked 12, 1, and 2; Dallas 1, 11, and 10; Cleveland 11, 4, and 1; and Houston 7, 12, and 14 across High, Medium, and Instant respectively. The pattern mirrors an earlier observation in the separate AI Index stock-selection experiment, where reasoning depth materially changed portfolio weighting. In that comparison, 19 of the 30 Dow Jones component weights differed. Across the two domains, the same structural question appears: reasoning depth may affect allocation more strongly than selection. This does not yet establish that reasoning depth alone caused the differences. The natural-use experiment also allowed the reasoning configurations to differ in search breadth, information selection, evidence weighting, and stochastic path. What it does establish is that a user-facing configuration change can coincide with large changes in confidence or allocation even when headline choices remain mostly stable. Provisional cross-domain hypothesis AI reasoning depth may have a larger effect on allocation decisions-confidence, capital, priority, or risk weighting-than on categorical selections themselves.
